meta.blurb: A poor weaver's son became one of the richest men in America, then wrote an essay asking what the rich owe the rest of us. Read Andrew Carnegie's bold, famous and much-argued answer: give it away, wisely, while you are alive.
meta.bible: Andrew Carnegie: born in Dunfermline, Scotland, in 1835; moved to Pennsylvania in 1848; steel manufacturer; died at Lenox, Massachusetts, in August 1919, aged eighty-three. The Gospel of Wealth: his essay of 1889, first printed in the North American Review under the title Wealth; a British editor reprinted it as The Gospel of Wealth. Dunfermline: Scottish town of weavers. Scotland. Pittsburgh: city in Pennsylvania where the family settled. Pennsylvania. Colonel James Anderson: a gentleman who lent books from his private library to working boys. Thomas Scott: manager at the Pennsylvania Railroad who hired Carnegie in 1853. Homestead: the steel works where a deadly fight took place in 1892; Carnegie was in Scotland at the time. John Pierpont Morgan: the banker who bought Carnegie's steel company in 1901 for about 480 million dollars; it became part of United States Steel. Carnegie Hall: New York concert hall, opened 1891. Peace Palace: building at The Hague, helped by his gift. Carnegie Corporation of New York: foundation he founded in 1911. Cornell and Johns Hopkins: universities he praised. Rockefeller: another rich American who built a foundation. Fixed facts: Carnegie paid for more than 2,500 libraries; he gave away about 350 million dollars, roughly ninety percent of his fortune; he named three ways to use surplus wealth: leave it to family, leave it at death for public use, or give it in life; he preferred the third; he wrote that the man who dies thus rich dies disgraced; he thought only about nine hundred and fifty dollars in every thousand given as charity was wisely spent. Voice and tone: clear, balanced and thoughtful; set out what Carnegie said, then name fairly what critics and defenders say; each beat gives one idea.

B1B2: In 1889 a rich Scottish-American businessman named Andrew Carnegie wrote an essay with a bold question in it. What, he asked, should a person do with a very large fortune once he has made it?
Andrew Carnegie was born in 1835 in Dunfermline, a Scottish town known for its weavers. His father worked at a hand loom, and when machines took over the trade the family fell on hard times.
In 1848 the family crossed the Atlantic and settled near Pittsburgh in Pennsylvania. At the age of twelve, Andrew started work in a cotton mill, changing bobbins for very low pay.
Andrew soon became a messenger boy for a telegraph office, where he learned quickly. In his free time he borrowed books from the private library that Colonel James Anderson shared with working boys.

In 1853 Thomas Scott, a manager at the Pennsylvania Railroad, hired Andrew as his secretary and telegraph operator. Andrew learned fast, saved his money, and began to put it into businesses that were growing.
In the 1870s Carnegie turned to steel, which was used for rails, bridges and buildings. By running his steelworks carefully and keeping costs low, he built one of the largest companies in America.

Carnegie's essay was first printed in a magazine called the North American Review, under the plain title Wealth. A British editor later reprinted it as The Gospel of Wealth, and that is the name it keeps today.
Carnegie began by naming what he called the problem of his age. How should wealth be used so that rich and poor can still feel bound together as one community?
Carnegie looked back to an older time, when a master craftsman worked beside his apprentices. They often ate the same food and lived in much the same kind of house.
Then came large factories with hundreds of workers, and the owner could no longer know each one of them. The distance between his way of life and theirs grew very wide.

Carnegie pointed out that cheap goods had put comfort within reach of ordinary people. The laborer, he said, had more comforts than the farmer of earlier days, and the farmer had more than the landlord.

The contrast between the millionaire's palace and the labourer's cottage, Carnegie wrote, measures the change that civilisation has brought. He believed this change should be welcomed and not mourned.
Carnegie accepted what he called the law of competition. It is sometimes hard on the person who loses, he admitted, but he believed it was best for the whole human race.

Carnegie thought that private property, free competition and the freedom to earn were the foundations of progress. He did not like plans to put all property in common, because he thought they would remove the reward for effort.
Carnegie saw that great fortunes gather in the hands of a few able businessmen. This is natural, he said, because only a few people have the skill to build large companies.
What should be done with a great fortune once a family's needs have been met? Carnegie said there are only three ways to deal with it, and he judged them one by one.
The first way is to leave the whole fortune to one's own family. Carnegie thought this was unwise, because a huge inheritance often weakens the talents and ambitions of the children who receive it.
The second way is to leave money for good causes when one dies. Carnegie did not like this plan either, because wills are often argued over in court, and the money may never do what its owner wished.

Carnegie supported very high taxes on large estates when their owners died. He said that of all taxes this seemed the wisest, because it would encourage the rich to use their money well during their lives.
The third way is to give while you are alive, and Carnegie praised it above the others. The giver can see the results of his gift and can correct mistakes, which no dead person can do.
Carnegie described the man of wealth as a kind of trustee, or agent, for his poorer neighbours. His extra wealth, in this view, is a trust fund that he must spend for their benefit.
The first duty of a rich person, Carnegie said, is to live simply and to avoid showy displays of his money. He should set a good example by his quiet way of life.
The second duty is to provide moderately for the real needs of those who depend on him. Carnegie meant a comfortable life for the family, not a vast fortune that would spoil its children.
The third duty is to treat all extra money as a trust fund and to spend it where it will do the most good. In Carnegie's view the rich man could do this better than the poor could for themselves.

Carnegie wrote one of the most famous lines in his essay, that the man who dies thus rich dies disgraced. He meant a rich person who had held on to a great fortune and never used it for the common good.
Carnegie warned that giving money without thought can do more harm than good. He guessed that nine hundred and fifty dollars in every thousand given to charity were spent unwisely.
Carnegie said that the main thing in giving is to help those who will help themselves. Money should not make people lazy, but should give hard-working people a better chance.
Carnegie wrote that the best way of helping a community is to put ladders within its reach. People with ambition and talent can then climb up by their own effort.
Carnegie named universities and colleges as one of the best uses of wealth. A great college, he said, gives talented young people a chance to rise, whatever their families may own.
Carnegie considered the free library the best gift that a community could receive. It helps only those who take the trouble to use it, which is exactly the kind of help he wanted to give.
Carnegie usually paid for the building, but the town had to provide the land. It also had to promise to pay each year to run the library, so that it belonged to the community.
Carnegie also listed hospitals, medical schools and laboratories among the good uses of wealth. They improve health and knowledge for everyone, and not just for the person who pays.
Carnegie also supported public parks and gardens, galleries and museums. These give ordinary families beauty and rest that they could not buy for themselves.
Carnegie thought that fine music should be part of ordinary life, so he included concert halls in his list. The famous Carnegie Hall in New York, which opened in 1891, was built with his money.
Carnegie also named swimming baths, which gave city families a safe place to wash, exercise and play. In the crowded towns of his time, many homes had no bath at all.
Carnegie listed church buildings among his gifts, and he paid for thousands of organs in churches. He thought that a pleasant meeting place could do much good for a whole neighbourhood.
Carnegie suggested that giving wisely takes as much thought as earning. A donor should ask where each gift will do the most lasting good.
Carnegie believed that a large sum spent on one lasting good does more for a people than the same sum shared out in small amounts. A library or a college can serve thousands of people for many years.
Carnegie believed that the wealth of a few people could become, in the best sense, the property of the many. He saw this as a way to solve the problem of rich and poor.
Carnegie ended his essay with a hope that this true gospel concerning wealth would one day solve the problem of rich and poor. He wished for peace on earth and goodwill among men.

In 1901 Carnegie sold his steel company to the banker John Pierpont Morgan for about 480 million dollars. It became part of a new giant, United States Steel, and Carnegie, who was sixty-five, turned to giving.

Over the next years Carnegie paid for more than 2,500 libraries, as well as colleges, research and the Peace Palace at The Hague. In 1911 he created the Carnegie Corporation of New York to carry on his giving.

Critics point to Homestead, Pennsylvania, where in 1892 workers at Carnegie's steel works fought hired guards and several men were killed. Carnegie was in Scotland at the time, but many people blamed him for his company's harsh policy.
Critics argue that gifts, however generous, are no substitute for fair wages and fair taxes. They also ask why one rich man should decide what the whole public needs.

Defenders reply that Carnegie did not just talk about giving, because he really gave away most of his fortune. They say that the libraries helped countless people, who might never have owned a book otherwise.
Carnegie died in 1919 at the age of eighty-three, at his summer home in Massachusetts. By then he had given away about 350 million dollars, which was most of his fortune.

Carnegie's ideas helped to create what we now call modern philanthropy, the giving of money for the public good. Large foundations, which give money to schools, science and health, grew up in the years after him.
Today, more than a century later, people still argue about Carnegie's ideas. Some say that the rich should give more freely, and others say that governments should tax them and spend for everyone.
A reader does not need to be a millionaire to learn from Carnegie. We can ask how our own time, skills and spare money might help others to help themselves.
The lesson of The Gospel of Wealth is that great wealth carries a duty. Live simply, provide modestly for your family, and give the rest in your lifetime, wisely, to help others to climb.
C1C2: In June 1889 the steel manufacturer Andrew Carnegie, by then one of the richest men in America, published an essay that opened with a question that few of his fellow millionaires had ever asked in public. What, he wondered, is the right way to use a great fortune, and what duty does it place on the person who owns it? His answer was soon given a famous name, The Gospel of Wealth, and it is still argued about today.

Andrew Carnegie was born in 1835 in Dunfermline, a Scottish town famous for its weavers, and his father made cloth by hand on a loom in the family home. When steam-powered factories began to put such weavers out of work, the family fell into hardship and decided to look for a better life across the sea. The childhood left him with a lifelong respect for hard work and for education.

The Carnegies crossed the Atlantic in 1848 and settled near Pittsburgh, in Pennsylvania, where Andrew's father and the boy himself both looked for work. At twelve years old Andrew became a bobbin boy in a cotton mill, spending long days at the machines for wages that were very small. It was a hard beginning, but it taught him something about how factories run and what it is like to work in them.

Andrew soon moved from the factory to a telegraph office, where he worked as a messenger and learned the wires so well that he was promoted to operator. In his free hours he read widely, thanks to a local gentleman, Colonel James Anderson, who opened his private library of about four hundred books to working boys on Saturdays. Carnegie never forgot that kindness, and it later shaped the way he gave away his money.

In 1853 Thomas Scott, a senior manager at the Pennsylvania Railroad, hired the young telegrapher as his assistant, and Andrew learned a great deal about management by watching how a large organisation was run. He saved what he could, invested in growing companies and learned how to judge which ventures were sound. By his early thirties he was already comfortably well off, with enough money to think about building a business of his own.

In the 1870s Carnegie turned to steel, the strong new metal that was beginning to replace iron in rails, bridges and buildings. By adopting the latest methods, watching every cost and choosing talented partners, he built a company whose mills produced steel more cheaply than almost anyone else's. The profits made him one of the richest men in America, and they raised the question that his essay set out to answer.

The essay appeared in 1889 in the North American Review, a respected American magazine, where it carried the plain title Wealth. A British editor then reprinted it under the name by which it has been known ever since, The Gospel of Wealth, a title that suggests good news, though readers have long argued about whom the news was meant for. Carnegie later gathered it into a book of essays that carried the same name, and the book spread his ideas still further.

Carnegie opens with what he calls the problem of the age, which is the proper use of wealth, so that the bonds of brotherhood may still hold the rich and the poor together in harmony. He feared that if great fortunes were used badly, the gap between those who have much and those who have little would become a source of bitterness. The rest of his essay, whatever one thinks of it, is his long and carefully reasoned answer to this single question.

In the earlier time that Carnegie described, a master craftsman worked in the same small shop as his helpers, and the two lived in houses that were not very different. They ate at similar tables and wore similar clothes, so that the distance between employer and worker was short. That way of life was close and friendly, he admitted, but it was also very poor in comforts and goods.

With the growth of large factories and mass production, Carnegie said, the master could no longer know all his workers, and the distance between the owner's way of living and the workman's became enormous. The relationship, once personal and direct, became chiefly a matter of wages and contracts between people who were strangers to each other. He treated this change as a fact of the age, and he thought it useless to wish it away.

Carnegie did not think the new order was all loss, for the same factories that created great fortunes also produced cheap goods and made comfort common. What had once been a luxury for the rich, he said, had become an ordinary necessity, so that the labourer of his day was better supplied than the farmer of an earlier time, and the farmer better than the landlord. Books and pictures that a king could once hardly have obtained, he added, could now be found in many houses.

The contrast between the palace of the millionaire and the cottage of the labourer, Carnegie wrote, measures the change that civilisation has brought. He insisted that this change was not to be deplored but welcomed as highly beneficial, because it had raised the general standard of living and made possible every advance in learning and the arts. Readers then and now have disagreed with him, and he did not deny that the price was sometimes hard on those at the bottom.

Carnegie accepted without hesitation what he called the law of competition, the struggle of businesses to outdo one another in quality and price. It is sometimes hard on the individual, he admitted, since some lose their jobs or their companies, yet he believed it was best for the human race because it rewards the ablest and brings cheaper and better goods to everyone. Whether that claim is fully true has been argued ever since, and many economists would add that competition works best when it is fair.

Carnegie called individualism, private property, the accumulation of wealth and the law of competition the highest results of human experience, and he rejected the schemes of reformers who wished to hold all property in common. Such plans, he argued, would remove the reward for effort and talent, and thus the strongest reason for people to work and to improve. He was therefore not asking the wealthy to give up their property, but to use it in a particular way.

Carnegie observed that the new order tended to concentrate wealth in the hands of a few people, and he argued that this was natural because only a few have the rare gift of organising vast enterprises. Those same talented people, he added, were likely to be wiser administrators of surplus wealth than the masses would be if the money were simply divided among them. This is a controversial claim, and many readers today would ask who decides which people are the wisest.

Carnegie argued that a surplus fortune can be dealt with in only three ways, and he set them out as plainly as a lawyer lists the terms of a contract. It can be left to the owner's family, it can be bequeathed for public purposes after his death, or it can be administered by the owner himself during his lifetime for the good of the community. He examined each of these in turn, and his verdict was severe on the first two and full of praise for the third.

To leave great wealth to one's children, Carnegie argued, is usually a mistake, for an easy fortune tends to deaden the talents and energies of the young people who receive it. He believed that most heirs would be better off if they had to make their own way, and that the world would profit more if the money went to public purposes. He noted too that the sons of the rich, having never learned the value of money, too often waste the fortunes they receive.

The second way, bequeathing great sums for public purposes at death, seemed to Carnegie only a little better, for the wishes of the dead are often misunderstood or argued over in the courts. He implied that it is no great credit to give what one can no longer keep, since a gift made only at death costs the giver nothing. Wealth, in his view, should not wait for a funeral before it does good.

Carnegie went so far as to approve heavy taxes on large inheritances, calling death duties the wisest of all forms of taxation. By taxing great estates at death, he said, the state marks its condemnation of the selfish millionaire's unworthy life, and gives wealthy people a strong reason to put their money to use while they are alive. It was a remarkably bold thing for a millionaire to say in public, since many wealthy men of his day were deeply suspicious of any new tax.

The third way, giving away surplus wealth during one's lifetime, was the one Carnegie held up as the best and the only wise choice. A living giver can see where the money goes, learn from experience and correct his mistakes, while a gift left in a will must be trusted to strangers. It also puts the rich person's own judgment and effort to work for the public, and thus makes the whole fortune a source of good.

The wealthy person, Carnegie wrote, should become the mere trustee and agent of his poorer brethren, holding his surplus fortune on their behalf and spending it as he judges best for the community. In his eyes, the money is not so much his own property as a responsibility that comes with his ability. The idea has a noble sound, though critics have asked who gave the trustee his authority, and who may hold him to account.

The first duty of the man of wealth, in Carnegie's list, is to set an example of modest, unostentatious living, shunning display and extravagance. A rich person who flaunts his fortune, he implied, invites envy and wastes resources that could do real good, whereas one who lives plainly shows that wealth is a trust and not a toy. It is a striking rule from a man who owned a castle in Scotland, as his critics were quick to notice.

The second duty is to provide moderately for the legitimate wants of those who depend on the rich man, such as his wife and children, and Carnegie was careful to say that this does not mean heaping fortunes upon them. A family ought to be kept comfortable and well educated, he thought, but anything beyond that should be treated as surplus. The line between a reasonable provision and an excessive one, of course, is left for each person to draw.

The third duty, and the heart of the essay, is to regard all surplus revenue as trust funds that must be administered in the way most likely to produce beneficial results for the community. The rich man, Carnegie claimed, brings superior wisdom, experience and ability to the task, and may do for the poor what they would not or could not do for themselves. Today that confidence in the superior wisdom of the rich is the part of the argument that many readers find hardest to accept.

Carnegie summed up his argument in a sentence that has been repeated ever since, which is that the man who dies thus rich dies disgraced. He meant that a person who spends a lifetime gathering a fortune and leaves it behind, unspent for the public good, has failed in his chief duty. The line was meant to shock, and it did, for it asked the most successful people of the age to measure themselves by what they gave.

Giving, Carnegie warned, is not automatically a virtue, for he believed that careless charity may cause the very evils it tries to cure. Of every thousand dollars spent in so-called charity in his day, he guessed, perhaps nine hundred and fifty were spent unwisely, because gifts to those who could work often encouraged idleness. His readers were therefore asked not only to be generous but also to be thoughtful about the effects of their generosity.

In bestowing charity, Carnegie wrote, the main consideration should be to help those who will help themselves, for the aim is to lift the willing rather than to support the idle. A gift that makes a person dependent does him no favour, whereas one that opens a door for his own effort may change his life. Modern aid workers, who speak of teaching people to fish rather than handing them fish, would recognise the thought.

The best means of benefiting the community, Carnegie said, is to place within its reach the ladders upon which the aspiring can rise, such as libraries, schools, parks and halls where people may improve their minds. He held that the poor do not need to be given everything, but they do need a fair chance to use their own gifts. The image of the ladder has become the most memorable idea in the essay, and it remains the standard by which many gifts are judged.

Among the best fields for giving, Carnegie placed the founding of universities and colleges, praising donors who had endowed institutions such as Cornell and Johns Hopkins. A good college, he thought, serves the whole community by training talent that would otherwise be wasted, and it does so for generations. He later extended the same thinking to technical schools, and the institution that grew from his Pittsburgh school still bears his name.

Of all the gifts that a person of wealth could make, Carnegie ranked the free public library highest, and he remembered his own Saturdays in Colonel Anderson's library as proof of its worth. A library gives nothing to those who do not want to learn, yet it gives everything to those who do, and so it helps only those who help themselves. In his lifetime he paid for more than two thousand five hundred of them around the world.

Carnegie did not simply hand over a building and leave, for his usual condition was that the town should provide the site and promise a yearly sum from taxes to pay for staff and books. This meant that the library would be owned and supported by the people it served, and that the gift would not become a burden on the donor for ever. Many communities took pride in these buildings, and many Carnegie libraries are still in use today.

Carnegie also placed hospitals, medical colleges and scientific laboratories among the best fields for giving, because they improve health and knowledge for the whole community and not only for the donor's neighbours. A discovery made in a well-equipped laboratory, he believed, may relieve suffering for generations. His own later gifts included funds for research, and the institutions he set up continue to support science today.

Public parks, picture galleries and museums were also high on Carnegie's list, since they bring beauty, refreshment and refinement into the lives of people who could never afford such things for themselves. A park, he argued, is a gift enjoyed equally by the rich and the poor, and a gallery gives a working family a view of what the best artists have achieved. Such gifts, in his opinion, improve the taste of a whole people and not just that of the donor's class.

Music also had a place in Carnegie's plan, and he included concert halls among the best gifts to a city because they allow large audiences to hear great performers together. The most famous example is Carnegie Hall in New York, which opened in 1891 and has welcomed many of the world's finest musicians. It shows how a single large gift, wisely made, can serve a community for well over a century.

Swimming baths appear in the same list, for in the crowded cities of the nineteenth century many homes had no bath at all, and a public pool offered a place to wash, to exercise and to enjoy the water. Carnegie had in mind not luxuries but improvements to daily life that ordinary people could use every day. He was thinking of the whole range of everyday needs, including health, learning and enjoyment, and not only of the great showpieces.

Church buildings were another field that Carnegie supported, and he is remembered for paying for several thousand organs in churches across the English-speaking world. He valued such places as centres of community life, where people meet, sing and support one another, and he gave to congregations of many different kinds. In his view a pleasant and dignified building did good to a whole neighbourhood, whatever its beliefs.

Carnegie suggested that giving well takes as much thought and effort as earning, and he asked the wealthy to study their gifts with the same care that they gave to their businesses. A donor must ask what a gift will achieve in ten or fifty years, who will look after it, and whether it will help people to rise by their own exertions. A hasty gift, however kind its intention, may leave little of lasting value behind it when the money has been spent.

Carnegie's central argument for his method was that a great fortune, spent wisely by one person, can do far more for the community than the same money scattered in small sums among its members. A pound or a dollar handed out is soon spent, he said, while a library, a college or a hospital continues to give benefit year after year. He believed that even the poor, if they considered the matter calmly, would come to agree with this view.

When wealth is administered in this way, Carnegie concluded, the surplus of the few becomes in the best sense the property of the many, since it is used for the common good and its benefits flow to the whole community. The problem of the rich and the poor, he claimed, would then be solved without the conflict that other reformers expected. It was a hopeful vision, and it was offered with complete sincerity, though its critics have doubted that it could ever be enough.

Carnegie closed his essay on a note of high hope, calling his teaching the true gospel concerning wealth and predicting that obedience to it would some day solve the problem of the rich and the poor. He ended with the old wish for peace on earth and goodwill among men, and he plainly believed that his plan could help to bring it about. Whether his hope has been fulfilled is a question that readers have asked ever since.

In 1901 Carnegie sold his steel company to the banker John Pierpont Morgan for about 480 million dollars, and the business became part of a new giant, the United States Steel Corporation. Carnegie, then sixty-five, retired from business and announced that he would devote the rest of his life to the task he had described in his essay. For the first time the author of the gospel of wealth had a very large surplus to give, and the world would see what he did with it.

In the years after 1901 Carnegie gave with remarkable energy, paying for more than two and a half thousand libraries, a technical school in Pittsburgh, scientific research, the Peace Palace at The Hague and church organs in thousands of towns. In 1911 he founded the Carnegie Corporation of New York, with a large endowment, so that his giving could continue after his death in the same spirit and under wise management. By the end of his life he had given away most of his fortune, and he had sought to do so while he was alive to see the results.

The most serious criticism of Carnegie's reputation comes from the steel works at Homestead, Pennsylvania, where in 1892 a dispute between the company and its workers ended in a battle with hired guards in which several men were killed. Carnegie was in Scotland at the time, but he had left his manager in charge, and many Americans felt that a man who preached about duty to the community had shown too little duty to his own workers. The event did lasting damage to his name, and it is still discussed alongside his libraries.

Critics have raised further objections, arguing that charity cannot take the place of fair wages and that a rich donor may decide for the public what it needs without being asked. They add that taxes would put the same money under the control of elected representatives, and that gathering vast fortunes and then giving them away is not the only road to good results. These are serious questions, and Carnegie's essay, which is so clear about its own answer, makes them easier to ask.

Defenders answer that Carnegie not only taught the duty of giving but also practised it on a vast scale, and that millions of ordinary people used his libraries to educate themselves as he himself had done. They add that the idea that great wealth carries great responsibility, which was not widely accepted in his day, has since become a common expectation of the very rich. Whatever one thinks of the man, the argument goes, he used his money in a way that helped many.

Andrew Carnegie died in August 1919, at the age of eighty-three, at his summer home in Lenox, Massachusetts, having given away about 350 million dollars, roughly ninety percent of his fortune. Whatever one may think of his methods, he did very largely act on his own advice, and the world he left behind is full of buildings and funds that carry his name. By his own standard, at least, he had tried to avoid dying rich, and he had largely succeeded in that aim.

Carnegie's essay did much to shape what we now call philanthropy, the organised giving of large sums for public purposes through foundations and trusts. Other wealthy Americans, among them the oil magnate John Rockefeller, created their own great foundations in the following years, and in later times many rich people have publicly promised to give away most of their wealth. The habits of mind that he described have become so familiar that we sometimes forget that someone had to argue for them.

The debate that Carnegie began is far from over, for people still disagree about whether the rich should be trusted to decide how to use their fortunes, or whether governments should collect taxes and spend them under public control. Some argue for a mixture of the two, in which rich donors give freely and governments also tax fairly. It is a lasting question, and his essay remains a clear starting point for anyone who wants to think about it.

One need not own a steel company to learn something from Carnegie's essay, for his central questions apply to any person who has more than he needs. Whether the surplus is money, time or skill, we may ask how it can be used to build the strength and opportunities of others rather than to create dependence. A small gift that opens a door for a neighbour may do as much good as a large one that is carelessly given.

The lesson of The Gospel of Wealth is that wealth is a trust, and that a person who has gathered more than he needs should use the surplus wisely, and in his lifetime, for the common good. Carnegie wished the rich to live modestly, to provide sensibly for their families and to give people ladders by which the willing may rise. It was a bold idea in 1889, and whether or not one accepts all of it, the question it asks, what do we owe to others, remains as important as ever.
